name: Ironthread Shelf Hauler's Full Kit
description: A working rig assembled for repeated heavy labor in corrosive conditions — the kind of outfit that gets worn six days a week, washed when there's water, and repaired the same night it tears. The primary garment is a full-coverage boilersuit in heavyweight faded olive drab, the fabric stiffened from years of oil, industrial sealant, and repeated acid-rain exposure into something approaching light armor. The chest panel has a large rectangular acid-shield patch in charcoal gray, edges sealed with a bead of industrial adhesive that's cracked and re-applied so many times it forms a topographic ridge around the patch's perimeter. Both knees are likewise reinforced — the right with rubberized canvas, the left with a section of industrial conveyor belting cut to fit and secured with heavy rivets. The suit's left sleeve has been cut away at the shoulder and replaced with a chrome-compatible open channel — the wearer has a partial arm augmentation, and the channel is lined with a strip of anti-friction neoprene to prevent the chrome edge from catching on fabric. Beneath the suit, a compression underlayer in gray spandex-blend manages sweat and minor impact. Over the suit in cold conditions, a quilted over-vest in faded black adds thermal mass, its front closure a row of industrial snaps, two of which are mismatched replacements. Boots are heavy-duty, triple-resoled Shelf work boots, the uppers stitched with waxed cord in three different colors where seams have been re-done, the toe box packed with a steel plate cut from a sheet of scrap. A wide back-support belt in reinforced nylon completes the lower kit. The face is partially protected by a half-mask respirator in scuffed gray plastic, worn around the neck when not in use, its filter cartridge visibly old and marked with a hand-scratched date.
functionality: Full-body acid and corrosive splash protection; chrome-compatible open sleeve channel with neoprene lining; steel-reinforced toe box; back-support belt for heavy lifting; integrated respirator for airborne hazard environments; thermal vest layer for temperature regulation; knee reinforcement for kneeling work on hard surfaces
what_it_says: Pure labor. This rig says the wearer moves things, fixes things, hauls things — and has been doing it long enough that the suit itself is a record. The chrome-compatible sleeve channel is notable: this person has augmentation, which costs money, which means either sacrifice or debt. The aug may be the most expensive thing they own, and the suit is built around protecting it.
worn_by: aug-users who can't afford Tier 2 work
people working informal construction in the Shelf's lower zones
manufacturer: Base suit is surplus Crucible industrial workwear, heavily modified; vest is self-made; aug channel modification done by a local fabricator
price_range: Φ 25–55 complete kit; base suit Φ 8–15 surplus
story_hooks: The hand-scratched date on the respirator filter is six months past its safe-use window. The wearer knows this. Replacement filters cost Φ 4 and that money is going somewhere else.

The chrome sleeve channel was fabricated by a specific underground aug-tech in the Shelf's transit underbelly — and that person has since disappeared, which is information someone with resources would pay for.

The acid-shield patch on the chest was applied after an industrial accident that officially never happened — a Crucible subsidiary spill that was covered up. The patch is evidence. The wearer is evidence.

physical_description.visual_profile: A heavily worn, purpose-built labor rig that reads as practical armor rather than fashion. The silhouette is blocky and utilitarian—broad-shouldered, reinforced at stress points, with visible patches and repairs creating an asymmetrical patchwork. The overall impression is of someone who works in hazardous conditions and trusts their gear with their life.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and accommodating—cut for movement and layering, with extra room across the chest and shoulders for the compression base layer beneath. The boilersuit hangs straight from the hips, designed for function over form. The over-vest sits loose enough to be donned quickly.
physical_description.primary_material: Heavyweight Crucible surplus industrial canvas boilersuit (faded olive drab, stiffened by years of chemical exposure); reinforcement panels in rubberized canvas and industrial conveyor belting; quilted synthetic insulation in the over-vest; neoprene anti-friction lining; nylon back-support belt; waxed cord stitching
physical_description.texture: Rough, weathered, and tactilely complex—the primary fabric is stiffened and slightly brittle from repeated exposure to oils and sealants. The acid-shield patch has a raised, cracked adhesive ridge. Conveyor belting section is textured rubber. Chrome channel lining is smooth neoprene. Quilting in the vest creates a padded, slightly rumpled surface.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant faded olive drab boilersuit; charcoal gray acid-shield patch with topographic adhesive ridging; black quilted over-vest; gray compression underlayer visible at openings; steel gray half-mask respirator; waxed cord stitching in three colors (pale tan, rust, dark brown)
physical_description.closures: Industrial snaps on the over-vest (two mismatched replacements evident); boilersuit appears to be standard front zip (worn and possibly seized); belt is buckle-fastened; boots laced with waxed cord
distinctive_features: Left shoulder cut away and fitted with chrome-compatible open channel (lined with neoprene) for partial arm augmentation
Large rectangular acid-shield patch on chest with cracked, re-applied adhesive bead forming visible ridges
Right knee reinforced with rubberized canvas; left knee reinforced with riveted industrial conveyor belting
Boots with triple-resoled uppers, steel plate toe box, and multi-colored waxed cord seam repairs
Half-mask respirator worn around neck, filter cartridge visibly aged with hand-scratched date marking
Visible compression gray spandex-blend underlayer at neck, cuffs, and aug channel opening
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4–5 salvage and working class. The garment is genuine industrial surplus and self-maintained, not aspirational. Every repair is visible and functional rather than aesthetic.
physical_description.cultural_context: Shelf hauler, heavy industrial labor, corrosive-environment worker. Wearing this signals someone who works in the GLMZ's ungoverned industrial zones—possibly a independent contractor or sub-grade laborer in chemical processing, scrap reclamation, or infrastructure maintenance. The augmentation channel indicates integration into corpo-adjacent work without corpo resources.
physical_description.condition_typical: Chronically weathered and patched. The garment is in active heavy use, repaired the same night it tears, washed infrequently due to water scarcity. Every visible panel tells a story of damage and repair. Not pristine, not collapsing—functional and hardened.
